hero.name: Sana
hero.who: runs a small online chikankari shop in Lucknow and loses whole weeks to setbacks

story.b: Sana sells hand-embroidered chikankari kurtas online from a small room above her father's shop in Aminabad, Lucknow. Six women from nearby lanes do the embroidery, and Sana handles photos, orders and packing. On Monday morning she finds a one-star review. The customer says the kurta looks different from the photo. Sana's stomach drops. She reads it eleven times. She stops posting, skips her packing schedule and snaps at Rukhsana aapa over a small thread colour. On Wednesday a courier loses two parcels, and she spends the evening crying on the terrace. By Friday she has not shipped a single order. Her younger brother Imran asks why the whole week stopped because of one comment. Sana has no answer.

ask.q: One review and two lost parcels have stopped Sana's whole week. What is the most useful thing for her to learn?
o: How to turn each problem into a next step instead of a reason to stop
How to avoid bad reviews completely by never selling to strangers
How to hide from setbacks until she feels ready again
ask.why: Bad reviews and lost parcels will keep coming in any business, so avoiding them or hiding until she feels better only stretches one bad day into a lost week. Learning to treat each problem as something to work with keeps her moving.

chapters.take: Setbacks are part of the work. The trouble is letting them stop it.

story.b: On Saturday, Sana opens the review again, but this time she tries a trick. She imagines it was written about her friend Nida's shop, not hers. Then she writes only the facts on a sticky note. One customer. One kurta. Colour looked different from the photo. No drama words, no story about her shop being doomed. Seen like that, it looks like a small, fixable problem. She checks the photo. The ring light makes the pastel pink look almost peach. That is not a disaster. It is a lighting issue. She replies politely, offers an exchange and reshoots the photo near the window in daylight. The customer thanks her. A week later, the same customer orders two more.

ask.q: A bigger shop copies Sana's best design, and she feels everything is ruined. What should she do first?
o: Post an angry message about them on Instagram right away
Assume her business is finished and stop designing
Write the situation in plain facts, as if it happened to a friend
ask.why: Panic makes a problem look bigger than it is, so angry posts and giving up both come from the drama, not the facts. Writing it plainly, as if advising a friend, shows what actually happened and what can be done next.

chapters.take: Describe the problem in plain facts. It usually shrinks.

story.b: Sana gets a stall at a crafts fair in Gomti Nagar. On the busiest evening, the stall lights flicker out, a crowd of customers is waiting, and a woman starts shouting that a kurta she bought online has a loose thread. People turn to stare. Sana feels her face burn and her words begin to race. Then she stops. She takes three slow breaths. She asks Imran to fetch the spare bulb from the scooter. She turns to the woman, looks at the kurta and agrees the thread is loose. She offers a free repair by Rukhsana aapa within two days. The woman calms down. Two customers who watched the whole thing buy kurtas before the stall closes.

ask.q: Imran's college presentation is tomorrow, and his slides crash in rehearsal. What advice should Sana give him?
o: Panic now so he takes it seriously enough
Breathe slowly, focus on the next small fix, and ignore the noise in his head
Cancel the presentation and blame the laptop
ask.why: Panic makes thinking harder right when he needs it most, and cancelling turns a fixable problem into a missed chance. Calm breathing and attention on the next single step help him make clear choices under pressure. Composure is control, not weakness.

chapters.take: When things go wrong, breathe first. Then fix the next small thing.

story.b: Sana wants her kurtas in proper boutiques outside Lucknow. For months she has waited for the right moment: a better website, a perfect catalogue, more followers. Now she decides to stop waiting. She makes a simple catalogue with ten designs and their prices and emails it to ten boutiques in Pune, Jaipur and Bengaluru. Seven do not reply. Two say no. One owner in Pune says the catalogue is nice, but the price list is confusing. The old Sana would have closed the laptop for a month. Instead she fixes the price list that same night and sends the catalogue to ten more shops. By the end of the month, two boutiques have placed small trial orders.

ask.q: Seven boutiques do not reply and two say no. What is Sana's best next step?
o: Use the one piece of feedback, fix it, and send to the next set of shops
Wait until she has a full website before trying again
Stop pitching, since boutiques clearly do not want her work
ask.why: Waiting for perfect conditions is how months disappear, and nine quiet answers do not prove her work is bad. Small steady actions, each improved by what she learned, build momentum. Movement creates chances that waiting never does.

chapters.take: Do not wait for perfect conditions. Take the next small step, then another.

story.b: In March, a Bengaluru boutique sends back half its order. The sizes are uneven. A medium from one embroiderer is bigger than a medium from another. Sana is embarrassed and angry, mostly at herself. Then she looks closer. The problem is telling her something. Her shop has no standard patterns, and every customer has quietly been guessing their size. She spends two weeks with a local tailor making proper paper patterns for each size and a clear size chart with photos. She trains the women to measure the same way. When she sends the order again, the boutique owner is impressed. Soon reviews start mentioning the fit. The returned parcel has become the thing her shop is known for.

ask.q: Sana's friend Nida lost a big wedding order because her delivery was late. What would help Nida most?
o: Forget it quickly and move on without thinking about it
Decide she is just unlucky with big orders
Ask what the delay reveals about her process, and fix that part
ask.why: Forgetting it wastes the lesson, and blaming luck leaves the same weak spot in place for next time. Looking at what the delay reveals, perhaps no spare days or one slow supplier, turns the setback into the exact improvement her business needs.

chapters.take: Every obstacle carries a lesson. Look for it before you look away.

story.b: In June, Sana's father falls ill and spends two weeks in hospital. The doctors say recovery will take time. Suddenly Sana is shuttling between the ward, the pharmacy and the workroom, and orders begin to pile up. She cannot do anything about the biggest problem in her life. She cannot make Abbu better faster. What she can choose is how she carries it. She tells her customers honestly that orders will take a little longer. She asks Imran and Rukhsana aapa to share the packing, and she talks to her friend Nida on the worst nights. She lets herself cry on the terrace sometimes, then goes back in. In the evenings, she sits beside her father and reads him the new reviews. He smiles at every one.

ask.q: Sana feels she must handle Abbu's illness and the whole shop alone, without telling anyone. What would serve her best?
o: Keep everything to herself so nobody worries
Accept what she cannot control, share the load and lean on people around her
Push on at full speed as if nothing has changed
ask.why: Some hardships cannot be fixed, only carried. Hiding the strain or pretending nothing has changed usually leads to burnout. Accepting the situation, asking family for help and talking to someone she trusts gives her the strength to keep going with patience.

chapters.take: Some things cannot be fixed. You can still choose how you carry them.

story.b: By autumn, Abbu is walking to the corner shop again with a stick, and the business is busier than ever. Five boutiques now stock Sana's kurtas, and half her competitors have copied the size chart. One afternoon a new one-star review appears. The parcel arrived late, the customer says. Sana reads it once. She writes the facts on a sticky note, checks the courier record, apologises and offers free shipping next time. Then she goes back to packing. The whole thing takes ten minutes. Imran notices and teases her about the week she once lost to a single comment. Sana laughs, tapes the sticky note to the wall, and asks him to fetch more tissue paper.

chapters.take: Problems still come. They just do not get to decide her week anymore.
